title: Detecting Misinformation: Identifying False News Spread by Political Leaders in the Global South
screen_reason: Observational study of the full public output of 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter (4,032,907 posts, 2018-2020). Reports quantitative shares of posts containing misinformation, shares of politicians who ever shared it, and shares of engagement and of views going to such posts, each with an explicit denominator, under three detection approaches. Meets the SHARING criterion (share of posts carrying misinformation and share of actors who shared any) and the EXPOSURE criterion (share of views to misinformation posts). The paper is partly methodological, but the descriptive prevalence numbers are reported as headline results (Table 2).

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders' social media posts containing misinformation, text-based (fact-check matching) approach
estimates.value_raw: Text 421 ... 0.0104 (Table 2); 'about 0.01% (421) of politicians' posts contain false stories'
estimates.denominator: 4,032,907 public posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook (1.5m), Instagram (1.1m) and Twitter (1.5m), January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: A post whose text matched (cosine similarity > .4 on TF-IDF vectors, after a Naive Bayes filter) one of 4,050 stories fact-checked as false by Boatos, and was then confirmed as a match by human coders
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: Using our text-based approach, about 0.01% (421) of politicians’ posts contain false stories.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 4,050 false stories scraped from Boatos, one of Brazil's six main fact-checking agencies (chosen because it publishes the verbatim text of the checked rumour, and validated against the other five agencies). Candidate posts were filtered by a Naive Bayes classifier (F1 .940-.954) and TF-IDF cosine similarity > .4, then every candidate was reviewed by two Portuguese-speaking coders independently with a third coder adjudicating disagreements and all positives; coders disagreed on 241 posts (5.8% of manually reviewed observations). An external fact-checking organisation reviewed 1,509 sampled posts: false-positive rate 8.3%, false-negative rate 1.2-7.6% for this approach.
estimates.moderator_quote: Leaders include the president, vice-president, cabinet members, governors, vice-governors, federal deputies, senators, and candidates for mayoral office in all state capitals in 2020 (N = 945). ... In total, we collected just over 4 million social media posts (1.5 million from Facebook, 1.1 million from Instagram and 1.5 million from Twitter).
estimates.notes: This is the paper's own (preferred) detection approach, so it is treated as the reference definition and the domain-based and Facebook-URL rows are marked as definition variants of it. Data span three years; year given as the 2019 midpoint of the January 2018 - December 2020 window. denom_scope political_news because the denominator is the complete public communication output of a defined class of political actors, not a topical keyword corpus.

estimates.value_raw: Text 421 15.4497 (Table 2); 'Our text-based approach reveals that 15% (146) of politicians have shared misinformation at least once'

estimates.definition: A politician at least one of whose posts was matched to a Boatos-fact-checked false story and confirmed by human review
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: Detection Total Pct. of Politicians Pct. of Posts from Politicians Approach Identified Sharing False News Sharing False News Text 421 15.4497 0.0104
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, p. 18 (narrative on p. 17-18: 'Our text-based approach reveals that 15% (146) of politicians have shared misinformation at least once')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: As for the post-level text-based row: matching against 4,050 Boatos-fact-checked false stories, machine filtering then human review by two independent Portuguese-speaking coders with third-coder adjudication (5.8% disagreement rate).
estimates.moderator_quote: because of publicly available electoral and administrative data, we have the full set of elected and appointed political leaders, and we can select from an extensive sampling frame
estimates.notes: Actor share (share of politicians who ever shared misinformation), the elite analogue of a 'share of users who shared any'. Table 2 gives the precise 15.4497% (= 146/945); the narrative rounds to 15%. denom_scope population because the denominator is the full census of the studied population of actors.

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders' social media posts containing misinformation, domain-based (root-domain list) approach
estimates.value_raw: Domain 38,695 ... 0.9595 (Table 2); 'The domain-based approach suggests a much larger share of posts containing misinformation (0.96%)'
estimates.denominator: 4,032,907 public posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter, January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: A post containing a hyperlink to one of 228 root domains drawn from URLs shared in Brazil and flagged as false by Facebook's third-party fact-checkers in the Facebook URLs dataset
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: The domain-based approach suggests a much larger share of posts containing misinformation (0.96%) and Facebook URLs approach indicates a much smaller share ( < 0.001%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 228 root domains (excluding common domains such as youtube.com, twitter.com, yahoo.com and one main newspaper) compiled from all URLs in the Facebook URLs dataset that were shared in Brazil and flagged as false by third-party fact-checkers; the dataset is partially limited to URLs shared at least 100 times. A fact-checker audit of a stratified sample found 44.05% of posts flagged by this approach were rated true or non-verifiable (false positives); a manual check of 200 flagged posts found 131 of 139 working links (95%) had never been fact-checked by any agency.
estimates.moderator_quote: we compile a list of all the URLs from Facebook’s URL dataset that were shared in Brazil, flagged as false by third-party fact-checkers and were available in Facebook’s URL dataset, which is partially limited to URLs that have been shared at least 100 times. We utilize both the exact URL from the dataset (N = 365) and the root domain (N = 228, excluding the common domains such as youtube.com, twitter.com, yahoo.com, and a main newspaper) from this list.
estimates.notes: Broader definition variant of the text-based post-share row: source-level rather than claim-level, so breadth is blank. The authors show this approach mostly captures hyperpartisan rather than strictly false content (44% false-positive rate against an external fact-checker) and by construction can only reach the 25% of posts that carry an external hyperlink.

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders who shared misinformation at least once, domain-based (root-domain list) approach
estimates.value_raw: Domain 38,695 50.5820 (Table 2); 'the domain approach finds that at least 50% (478) of politicians have done so'
estimates.denominator: 945 Brazilian political leaders with public social media accounts
estimates.definition: A politician who posted at least one hyperlink to one of the 228 root domains flagged as false in the Facebook URLs dataset
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: whereas the domain approach finds that at least 50% (478) of politicians have done so.
estimates.page_loc: Results section 5, p. 17-18; Table 2 gives the precise 50.5820
estimates.ground_truth_detail: As for the domain-based post row: 228 root domains from the Facebook URLs dataset flagged as false by third-party fact-checkers; high false-positive rate (44.05%) against an external fact-checker review.
estimates.moderator_quote: Out of the 478 politicians who were classified as sharing misinformation in the domain-based approach, 73.2% (350) were not identified as sharing false content in the text-based approach
estimates.notes: Broader definition variant of the text-based actor-share row (50.5820% = 478/945 versus 15.4497% = 146/945 for the same politicians and the same posts). The 35-point gap between the two is the paper's central methodological point.

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders' social media posts containing misinformation, Facebook-URL (exact URL) approach
estimates.value_raw: Facebook URL 50 1.4815 0.0009 (Table 2); 'Facebook URLs approach indicates a much smaller share ( < 0.001%)'
estimates.denominator: 4,032,907 public posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter, January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: A post containing one of the 365 exact URLs labelled false by third-party fact-checkers in Facebook's URLs dataset
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.page_loc: Table 2, p. 18 (narrative on p. 17: 'Facebook URLs approach indicates a much smaller share ( < 0.001%)')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 365 exact URLs from Facebook's URLs dataset that were shared in Brazil and flagged as false by Facebook's third-party fact-checking partners; the dataset only covers URLs shared at least 100 times, so coverage is limited by platform policy and by differentially private noise.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the Facebook-URL approach we also identify posts, across all platforms, that contained the exact URL (as opposed to the root domain) labeled as false in Facebook URLs dataset.
estimates.notes: Strictest definition variant. The tabulated percentage (0.0009) does not reconcile exactly with the tabulated counts (50/4,032,907 = 0.00124%); 0.0009 is kept because it is the value stated verbatim in Table 2 and the narrative independently reports '< 0.001%'. Confidence medium for that arithmetic discrepancy.

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders who shared misinformation at least once, Facebook-URL (exact URL) approach
estimates.value_raw: Facebook URL 50 1.4815 (Table 2); 'Facebook’s URL approach find that 1.48% (14) of politicians have shared misinformation at least once'
estimates.denominator: 945 Brazilian political leaders with public social media accounts
estimates.definition: A politician who posted at least one of the 365 exact URLs labelled false by third-party fact-checkers in Facebook's URLs dataset
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: In contrast to these two approaches, Facebook’s URL approach find that 1.48% (14) of politicians have shared misinformation at least once.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: As for the Facebook-URL post row: 365 exact URLs flagged false by Facebook's third-party fact-checking partners, restricted to URLs shared at least 100 times.
estimates.moderator_quote: Due to the reliance on website links, all politicians identified through the Facebook-URL approach were also identified via the domain approach.
estimates.notes: Strictest definition variant of the actor-share estimate (1.4815% = 14/945).

estimates.measure_type: % of political leaders' social media posts containing misinformation according to at least one of the three detection approaches
estimates.value_raw: using at least one of the methods employed (text, domain, Facebook URL), we detect false content in 0.9694% of posts
estimates.denominator: 4,032,907 public posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter, January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: A post flagged by any one of the three approaches: text matching to a Boatos-fact-checked false story, a hyperlink to a flagged root domain, or a flagged exact Facebook URL
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: Overall, using at least one of the methods employed (text, domain, Facebook URL), we detect false content in 0.9694% of posts, and these 0.9694% of posts represent about 1.4197% of all the online engagement to politicians’ posts in the period analyzed.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Union of three ground truths: Boatos fact-checked false stories matched at claim level with human review; a 228-root-domain list from the Facebook URLs dataset (source level); and 365 exact fact-checked URLs. Numerically the union is dominated by the domain-list component.
estimates.moderator_quote: out of the 38,695 posts identified using the text- or the domain-based approach, only 19 posts were identified by both approaches
estimates.notes: Union definition variant. Stated verbatim by the authors (not a sum computed here); classification_level mixed and breadth blank because the union combines claim-level fact-check matches with a source-level domain list.

estimates.measure_type: % of all online engagement with political leaders' posts that went to posts containing misinformation (any of the three approaches)
estimates.value_raw: these 0.9694% of posts represent about 1.4197% of all the online engagement to politicians' posts in the period analyzed
estimates.denominator: All online engagement (all reaction types combined across Facebook, Instagram and Twitter) with the 4,032,907 posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders, January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: Engagement accruing to posts flagged as containing false content by at least one of the three detection approaches
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: Overall, using at least one of the methods employed (text, domain, Facebook URL), we detect false content in 0.9694% of posts, and these 0.9694% of posts represent about 1.4197% of all the online engagement to politicians’ posts in the period analyzed.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Union of the three ground truths (Boatos fact-checked claims with human review; 228-domain list; 365 exact fact-checked URLs); engagement is the sum of all reaction types across the three platforms.
estimates.moderator_quote: We calculate user engagement by combining all types of reactions across the three social media platforms.
estimates.notes: Engagement-weighted counterpart of the 0.9694% union post share: misinformation posts attract about 1.5 times their share of reactions. Coded SHARING/content_share because the denominator is engagement (the governing rule maps engagement denominators to SHARING); flagged borderline because the engaging actors are the audience, not the politicians, and unit is set to 'exposure' for want of a closer option for reaction events.

estimates.measure_type: % of all views of political leaders' posts that went to posts containing misinformation
estimates.value_raw: only 0.08% of views are to posts with any misinformation
estimates.denominator: All views of the 4,032,907 posts by 945 Brazilian political leaders on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter, January 2018 - December 2020
estimates.definition: Views accruing to posts flagged as containing any misinformation by the detection approaches
estimates.misinfo_def: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false
estimates.source_quote: they are seen at lower frequencies than posts without misinformation (only 0.08% of views are to posts with any misinformation).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Union of the three ground truths (Boatos fact-checked claims with human review; 228-domain list; 365 exact fact-checked URLs). View counts come from CrowdTangle (Facebook, Instagram) and the Twitter Academic API.
estimates.moderator_quote: posts with misinformation tend to be seen (on average and in terms of medians) more often than posts without misinformation, but we do not find that posts with misinformation are seen disproportionately more relative to their size
estimates.notes: The source_quote is the contiguous tail of the sentence; a footnote and a page number interrupt its opening in the PDF text. In full it reads 'In terms of views, we also find that posts with misinformation tend to be seen (on average and in terms of medians) more often than posts without misinformation, but we do not find that posts with misinformation are seen disproportionately more relative to their size - in fact, they are seen at lower frequencies than posts without misinformation (only 0.08% of views are to posts with any misinformation).' The only view-weighted (consumption) estimate in the paper, so it is coded EXPOSURE (exposure_type proportion). The sentence does not restate which detection approach(es) generate the numerator; the surrounding paragraph is about the union of all three ('posts with any misinformation'), so it is coded as such. Confidence medium because the underlying approach and the exact view denominator are not spelled out.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'in over four million posts in our data, 75% did not include a hyperlink to an external domain' — a structural feature of the corpus, not a misinformation share; (2) overlap statistics (19 of 38,695 posts flagged by both text and domain approaches; 128 of 496 politicians flagged by both; 12.3%, 73.2%, 93.8%, 35.7% non-overlap rates) — measures of agreement between approaches, not prevalence; (3) the fact-checker audit percentages in Table 3 (false-positive rates 8.3% text vs 44.05% domain; false-negative rates 1.2-7.6% text vs 1.2-40.7% domain; naive-sample true negatives 96.6% and 95.81%) — instrument validity statistics computed inside stratified validation samples, not prevalence of misinformation in the corpus; (4) 'in 70% of posts, either the contents of the link or the text posted in social media, were politicized/partisan' and the 45%/15%/30% partisanship breakdown of 500 domain-flagged posts — partisanship coding, not veracity; (5) '95% (131 of 139) of stories linked in domain-flagged posts were not checked by any fact-checking agency' and '10.2% of posts with cosine similarity > 0.4 contained false stories' — figures computed inside a misinformation-flagged or filtered subsample rather than the full corpus; (6) the US comparison figure '8.5% in a US sample of social media users shared misinformation' — cited from Guess, Nyhan and Reifler (2020), not this paper's own estimate, so excluded under the rule against figures a paper cites from elsewhere; (7) 'posts containing misinformation using our text-based approach receive 10 times more engagement than posts without misinformation' — a ratio, not a share. Main uncertainty: Table 2's Facebook-URL post percentage (0.0009) does not reconcile with its own counts (50/4,032,907 = 0.0012), and the view-share sentence (0.08%) does not name its detection approach.

rob.design: Full-census observational study of the public social media output of all 945 Brazilian elected and appointed political leaders (president, vice-president, cabinet, governors, vice-governors, federal deputies, senators, and 2020 mayoral candidates in all state capitals), January 2018 - December 2020: 4,032,907 posts collected from CrowdTangle (Facebook 1.5m, Instagram 1.1m) and the Twitter Academic API (1.5m). Three detection approaches compared: (a) text-based — 4,050 verbatim false stories scraped from the Boatos fact-checking agency, a per-platform Naive Bayes classifier (test accuracy 92.40-96.07%, F1 .940-.954) to prune to 425,949 suspicious posts, TF-IDF cosine similarity > .4 to reach 4,102 posts, then manual review by two independent Portuguese-speaking coders with a third adjudicating (241 disagreements, 5.8%), yielding 421 false posts; (b) domain-based — 228 root domains flagged false in the Facebook URLs dataset; (c) Facebook-URL — 365 exact flagged URLs. External validation: a Brazil-based fact-checking organisation reviewed 1,509 posts in three stratified random samples (naive N=501, domain N=504, text N=504), giving false-positive rates of 8.3% (text) and 44.05% (domain) and false-negative rates of 1.2-7.6% (text) and 1.2-40.7% (domain). No response rate applies (behavioural census data). Acknowledged limits: dependence on fact-checkers' editorial choices, use of a single fact-checking agency for rumour text, and the domain approach's structural blindness to the 75% of posts without external links.
rob.item6_quote: Political misinformation, commonly understood to include both false news (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021) and politically biased or misleading content that is not undeniably false (Ross, Rand and Pennycook, 2021; Pennycook and Rand, 2019), has been associated with undesirable outcomes such as disruptive elections, political unrest, violence, and ethnic strife, among others
rob.item10_quote: Using our text-based approach, about 0.01% (421) of politicians’ posts contain false stories.
